newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Japan rejects U.S. charges on photofilm market.
newsitem.headline: Japan rejects U.S. charges on photofilm market.

text.p: Japan denied U.S allegations on Wednesday that its measures covering domestic photofilm and paper violated free trade laws, but agreed to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) setting up a panel to rule on the dispute.
In a statement issued by the Japanese trade mission in Geneva, Japan said its film market, shared by Fuji and Eastman Kodak, was the "mirror image" of that in the United States.
The Europeon Union joined the U.S. complaint against Japan as a third party, officials said.
Nobutoshi Akao, Japan's trade ambassador to the WTO, said that the purview of the neutral panel should be limited to examining Japanese measures specified in the U.S. request.
In a speech to the closed-door WTO Dispute Settlement Body, Akao also served notice that Tokyo reserved its right to ask the panel to make a ruling on its own terms of reference.

"The Government of Japan is convinced that all of the measures that the U.S. Government has raised are fully consistent with the Government of Japan's obligations under the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) 1994, and is willing to make that point clear through the panel deliberations in accordance with the WTO dispute settlement procedures," the Japanese trade mission in Geneva said in a statement.

"The U.S. Government's claims are totally contrary to the fact. The Government of Japan has never taken any governmental action with either the intention nor the effect of excluding imports from the consumer phhotographic film and paper markets in Japan," it added.

It said Fuji had a 67 per cent share of the Japanese market, against 10 per cent for Kodak. The U.S. company enjoyed 73 per cent of its home market while Fuji had just 12 percent of the American market, according to the Japanese statement.
"The market share of Kodak in Japan fluctuates completely based on the efforts of the company," it added.
Japan's statement criticised the U.S. allegations as being "overtly vague and broad" and said allowing such an issue to be brought to the WTO had "wide implications on future cases".
Akao, in his speech obtained by Reuters, said: "...we do not consider that the United States has duly identified some of the "specific measures' at issue.

"Therefore, we believe that...the scope of the deliberations by the panel should be limited to the measures which have been specified in the request; that is to say, the six laws identified in the request and the 10 measures listed in Attachment A excluding the 'Administrative Guidance of 1966".
